title: Fighting for the Four Freedoms: World War II
summary: Through the 1930s most Americans, remembering World War I, wanted no part of foreign conflicts, and Congress passed Neutrality Acts barring arms sales to warring nations even as Japan invaded China and Hitler swallowed much of Europe. After Germany overran France in 1940, Roosevelt edged the nation toward the Allies with 'cash and carry' sales, the Lend-Lease Act, and an oil embargo against Japan, while framing the coming struggle around the Four Freedoms—of speech and worship, from want and fear. Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, brought the United States fully into the war. After early disasters, the navy's victory at Midway turned the Pacific war, Soviet victory at Stalingrad broke Germany in the east, and the D-Day landings of June 1944 opened the drive that liberated western Europe.

At home, war mobilization accomplished what the New Deal never had: the gross national product more than doubled, unemployment vanished, and new federal agencies directed production, prices, and labor. Defense spending built up the West Coast and South, millions of women took industrial jobs symbolized by Rosie the Riveter, and union membership hit record highs. 'Freedom' saturated wartime culture, but Americans disagreed about its meaning—New Dealers proposed an Economic Bill of Rights and Congress passed the GI Bill, while business promoted 'free enterprise' and Hayek's Road to Serfdom armed postwar conservatism.

The war against Nazi racism made pluralism official rhetoric and assimilated European ethnics as loyal Americans, yet tolerance had sharp limits. The government interned more than 110,000 Japanese-Americans, most of them citizens, a policy the Supreme Court upheld in Korematsu. Mexican braceros filled labor shortages amid the zoot suit riots, while some 700,000 Black southerners joined a second Great Migration; A. Philip Randolph's march threat won the FEPC, and the double-V campaign launched the modern civil rights movement. Roosevelt died in April 1945, Germany surrendered in May, and after Truman ordered atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan gave up—leaving the United States the world's dominant power in a new order framed by Bretton Woods, the United Nations, and rising tension with the Soviet Union.
big_ideas: Isolationism and the Neutrality Acts gave way step by step—cash and carry, Lend-Lease, the oil embargo—until Pearl Harbor brought full American entry into the war.
World War II was a war of production: American industrial output overwhelmed the Axis, ended the Depression, and tied big business to a militarized federal government.
FDR's Four Freedoms defined the war's meaning but became contested ground between advocates of an expanded New Deal and champions of 'free enterprise.'
The war temporarily transformed women's work and permanently reshaped population patterns, fueling the West, the South, and a second Great Migration of Black southerners.
Japanese-American internment, upheld in Korematsu v. United States, was the era's gravest violation of civil liberties and showed wartime freedom's limits.
The double-V campaign, the FEPC, CORE, and works like An American Dilemma made Black equality a national issue and seeded the postwar civil rights movement.
Allied diplomacy at Yalta and Potsdam, the Bretton Woods system, the United Nations, and the atomic bomb established American global dominance and set the stage for the Cold War.

key_terms.def: FDR's January 1941 statement of war aims—freedom of speech and worship, freedom from want and fear—which became the central language of American purpose during the war.
Laws passed between 1935 and 1939 banning arms sales and travel involving warring nations, reflecting the isolationist mood of Depression-era America.
The 1941 law allowing the United States to supply arms to Britain, China, and later the USSR with repayment deferred, making America the 'arsenal of democracy' before formally entering the war.
Japan's December 7, 1941 surprise air attack on the U.S. Pacific fleet in Hawaii, which killed more than 2,000 servicemen and brought the United States into World War II.
The June 1942 naval battle in which U.S. forces, aided by broken Japanese codes, destroyed four enemy carriers and turned the tide of the Pacific war.
The June 6, 1944 Allied landing in Normandy under Eisenhower, the largest sea-land invasion in history, which opened the western front that liberated France.
Nazi Germany's systematic murder of six million Jews and over a million other victims, the culmination of Hitler's racial ideology and a horror that discredited theories of racial hierarchy.
The 1944 Servicemen's Readjustment Act, which gave veterans education benefits, unemployment pay, and low-cost mortgages, fueling postwar college enrollment and suburban growth.
A 1942 U.S.-Mexico agreement bringing Mexican contract laborers to American farms; it lasted until 1964 and brought in more than 4.5 million workers who could be deported at will.
1943 violence in Los Angeles in which sailors and police attacked Mexican-American youths, exposing the gap between wartime rhetoric of tolerance and reality.
The removal under Executive Order 9066 of more than 110,000 people of Japanese descent—two-thirds of them citizens—from the West Coast to guarded camps for most of the war.
The 1944 Supreme Court decision upholding internment as constitutional; Justice Jackson's dissent warned the precedent lay ready 'like a loaded weapon' for future abuse.
The wartime movement of roughly 700,000 Black southerners to northern and western industrial cities, far larger than the World War I migration, which reshaped urban America.
The Black press's demand for victory over fascism abroad and over segregation at home, capturing African-American attitudes toward a war fought in freedom's name.
FDR's 1941 order, issued to head off A. Philip Randolph's threatened March on Washington, banning discrimination in defense industries and creating the Fair Employment Practices Commission.
The 1944 meeting that made the dollar the world's key currency and created the World Bank and IMF, anchoring the postwar economic order to American leadership.

timeline.event: Japan launches full-scale war against China, including the massacre of civilians at Nanjing.
Britain and France appease Hitler at Munich after Germany annexes Austria and the Sudetenland.
Germany invades Poland after the Nazi-Soviet pact, and Britain and France declare war.
France falls to the German blitzkrieg; FDR wins an unprecedented third term and the first peacetime draft begins.
FDR delivers the Four Freedoms speech, Congress passes Lend-Lease, and Japan attacks Pearl Harbor on December 7, bringing the U.S. into the war.
Executive Order 9066 sends Japanese-Americans to internment camps; the U.S. Navy wins at Midway; CORE is founded.
Race violence erupts in the Detroit riot and Los Angeles zoot suit riots; Congress repeals Chinese exclusion.
Allied forces land at Normandy on D-Day; Congress passes the GI Bill; the Bretton Woods conference meets; the Court decides Korematsu.
The Big Three meet at Yalta; FDR dies and Harry Truman becomes president; Germany surrenders on V-E Day in May.
Atomic bombs destroy Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, Japan surrenders, and the United Nations Charter takes effect.

themes: America in the world: The war ended isolationism for good, committing the United States to global leadership through new institutions like the UN, World Bank, and IMF.
Politics and power: Wartime agencies, rationing, and unprecedented spending vastly enlarged the federal government and forged a lasting military-industrial partnership.
American and national identity: The fight against Nazi racism promoted pluralism and assimilated European ethnics, while internment and segregation revealed who remained outside full citizenship.
Migration and settlement: Defense jobs pulled millions to West Coast cities, Black southerners north and west in the second Great Migration, and Mexican braceros into southwestern fields.
Work, exchange, and technology: War production doubled the economy, brought women into industry, and yielded radar, computers, and the atomic bomb—technologies that defined the postwar world.
